questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Plane
questions.problem:
Find the orthogonal projection of the vector $x$ onto the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -6 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that $v$ and $w$ are linearly independent. 

The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}{v,w}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ v & w \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ -6 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 4 & 14\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}7 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}7 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -4 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the vector in the subspace spanned by ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ 
that is closest to the vector $x,$ where 

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 3 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ are linearly independent. 

The closest vector to $x$ in the subspace spanned by ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace, which is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]\,⇒\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}27 & -3 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{24}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 9\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6} \\ \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Verify whether the vectors ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent, and find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the vectors ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we verify whether ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 \\ -3 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -3 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⇒\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -3 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -3 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -3 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}14 & 9 \\ 9 & 6\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}10 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -3 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}6 & -9 \\ -9 & 14\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}10 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -3 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Verify whether the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3$ are linearly independent, and find the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace spanned by the vectors $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3 \},$ where
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069030/assets/226d83de1fff110426877af083e1aee5eac7f7de1244bb59f7f801aeea8ec6a5.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we verify whether $\mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3$ are linearly independent. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}4 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}↔{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 4 \\ 3 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-4){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & -2 & -10 \\ 0 & -3 & -15\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{3}{2}){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & -2 & -10 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x}.
$$

In our case, we have
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069030/assets/c051729499bde9389ad7e38ab91d3609c8153cbed59233f4b3e3e7ac9e9c2534.png)

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}26 & 8 \\ 8 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}18 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{14}[\begin{aligned}3 & -8 \\ -8 & 26\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}18 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
